Figure 5: Overview of CAS. (a) Under mid-execution instruction switching, strong visual priors can cause the policy to remain drawn toward a non-target trajectory, resulting in trajectory hijacking.
(b) Inference-time CAS identifies interfering non-target tasks, uses target–counterfactual action differences to determine where to steer, and trajectory proximity to determine how much to steer. In the red-to-blue block example, the hijacking task happens to coincide with the source task, but this need not hold in general. For clarity, the arrows show a single action from the predicted action chunk.
(c) Successful CAS-guided rollouts can be used for self-training (CAS-ST), and this process can be applied iteratively. The blue-boxed comparison illustrates the effect of CAS-ST: given the same observation, the policy produces more task-distinct actions after self-training.
